# Doctrine: Principles, Decision Guides, and Named Anti-Patterns

This document compresses the preceding argument into principles, decision
guides, and named anti-patterns for design reviews. Each principle is framed
by its downstream payoff: knowledge belongs in the model when it removes
interpretation, checking, or branching from consumers.

A register note before the principles: everything in this document is
**doctrine** — deliberately imperative defaults distilled from documented S7
behavior and observed ecosystem practice, but laws of neither. The
imperative mood is a choice: a crisp default you can overrule for stated
reasons is more useful in a design session than a hedge you can ignore.
"Always" and "never" here mean "strong default," and when a principle
collides with a real constraint, the earlier documents carry the reasoning
needed to make the trade explicitly.

## Principles

**Model meaning through representative designs.** Begin with the domain,
intended consumers, and a few representative values and operations. Record the
semantic atoms and laws those examples expose, then revisit both structure and
behavior. Meaning can be more stable than document shape, but it is discovered
iteratively rather than by completing a universal foundation first.

**Let construction retain evidence.** Boundary functions turn loose input
into representations that record what was learned, so downstream code can
demand those representations instead of re-checking raw contents.
Construction certifies only invariants visible at that boundary and preserved
by supported transformations; references inside an object and external facts
remain outside that certificate.

**Constructors normalize; validators verify; boundaries translate.**
Coercion, canonicalization, and version gating happen once, at the boundary.
Validators judge canonical values only, and stay pure and cheap because they
run on every property write. A validator accommodating multiple input shapes
is a parser in the wrong place, running forever.

**Give every invariant one authoritative home.** Place each law at the lowest
boundary that sees everything it mentions: external conformance at the wire,
parsing at the boundary, type on the
property class, local law in the property validator, cross-property law in
the class validator, cross-object law in the aggregate root, operation
legality in the mutator, developer invariants in assertions. Each rung
assumes the rungs below and duplicates none. A cheap duplicate deliberately
retained for better boundary diagnostics is a documented trade; a law found
on two rungs *by accident* is a bug waiting to be two different laws.
The governing test is the rule's **visibility horizon**. A channel range is
visible to one property; start-before-end needs the whole object; unique ids
need the collection; authorization needs the live authority. Below that
horizon the rule is uncheckable, while above it the rule runs too often and
couples code to context it does not need.

**Treat presence and default ownership as a contract.** Required in the
result, caller-supplied, nullable, `NA`-able, empty, defaulted, and omitted on
serialization are separate decisions. Record whether R, an external authority,
or the caller requesting materialization owns a default. One `optional` flag
cannot preserve these meanings.

**Treat constants as identity when instances cannot differ.** If two
instances of a class can never differ on a field, the field is part of what
the class *is*: model it as a computed property or inject it at serialization,
and keep it out of the constructor. Store it only when round-trip fidelity or
spec evolution demands that instances carry it.

**Represent alternatives as alternatives.** Flag fields, mutually
exclusive nullables, and mode strings are sum types flattened into products.
Give variants honest representation: concrete variant classes when identity,
fields, or behavior differ; enum properties when only the tag differs; unions
when one slot accepts several primitive or domain classes. Abstract parents
provide shared schema or protocol but do not seal a family. Loud fallbacks and
coverage tests detect unsupported known cases; they do not prove
exhaustiveness.

**Inherit for dispatch and substitutability; compose for structure.**
Parents contribute a property schema and a dispatch position to things that
genuinely are the parent. Everything else — nesting, reuse, independent
dimensions — is composition. Hierarchies stay shallow: abstract root,
concrete leaves, intermediate levels only when they add a genuine is-a
concept and either a useful dispatch position, shared invariant-bearing
schema, or structural exclusion of illegal states. Inherit from a base type
only when the object *is* that primitive.

**Co-design nouns and verbs.** Behavior belongs to generics, and interfaces
are generic sets plus laws. Design the verb vocabulary as deliberately as the
class graph. An
extension point is a set of generics an implementor must support *and* the
laws those methods must satisfy — write the laws down, executably where
possible. Let operations revise the representation when they reveal missing
distinctions. Reach for multiple dispatch when behavior genuinely varies
along two type axes.

**Choose lifecycle policy explicitly.** Editable values are revised through
replacement. Read-only snapshots are values whose public API forbids revision.
Reference owners coordinate shared identity, resources, or observable
lifecycles. Keep domain knowledge in values where possible, and document any
reference-valued payload because outer validation will not observe its
internal mutation.

These policies answer different questions. A **value** says that revision
produces another value. A **snapshot** says that the represented fact is
complete and the public API offers no revision, even though S7 replacement
machinery still exists underneath. An **owner** says that aliases must observe
one evolving process or resource. A chat may therefore own a live stream while
emitting completed turns as snapshots; the hybrid is explicit rather than an
exception hidden inside a nominally immutable object.

**Revise related properties together, through the front door.** Invariants
spanning several properties imply every update of those properties goes
through one grouped replacement (`S7::set_props()`), wrapped in a
transformation function. Guarantees hold for supported clients of the
exported surface; make the front door the easiest path.

**Use one authoritative meaning with deliberate projections.** When several
outputs encode the same knowledge — an expression and a legend; a class graph
and its documentation; a wire format and a pretty printer — designate one
canonical source and derive deliberate projections. This removes independently
maintained definitions and makes consistency testable; translators and
generators can still be wrong.

**Keep property access cheap and pure.** Getters compute derivations; they
never perform I/O, never mutate, never surprise. The moment `x@thing` can be
slow or effectful, the object stops being data in the reader's mind, and the
whole value-semantics reasoning collapses.

**Make generalized machinery earn its keep.** Every layer of indirection pays
rent by absorbing a demonstrated axis of variation. Apply the rule of three
to factories, metamodels, and framework layers, not to naming an important
domain concept. Delete machinery that no longer simplifies its consumers.

**Choose schema authority before generation strategy.** Validate against
external schemas with the schema ecosystem's own tools at the wire; read
foreign schemas as a census that can inform a hand-designed semantic model.
Generating a native transport facade may be appropriate when foreign flatness
is authoritative. When the package owns a semantic specification, generating
classes, validators, schemas, and documentation from it may also be
appropriate. Do not confuse either case with mirroring incidental foreign
structure without a consumer-driven reason.

The key distinction is between a **transport facade** and a **semantic
model**. A facade may intentionally preserve foreign names, optionality, and
nesting because exact interchange is its job. A semantic model collapses
structural duplicates, names domain distinctions, and serves native
operations. Some packages need both, joined by an explicit parser or adapter;
generation is then a maintenance technique, not evidence that the two layers
mean the same thing.

**Refuse to guess.** Where no correct behavior is known, an error beats a
default. sqlr states the reason perfectly in declining to ship an "ANSI SQL"
fallback dialect: an untestable default "would quietly accumulate behaviour no
database had ever accepted." The same logic condemns silent coercion of
ambiguous input, fallback branches for "unknown type," and any code path no
test can exercise against a real authority. A loud, early error is
information; a guess is deferred corruption.

**Check as early as the inputs allow, as late as the context requires.**
The value of a check is proportional to the cost of the work it gates.
Declarations should validate themselves at package load (a default violating
its own bounds is the author's bug, catchable before any user exists);
configurations should validate fully before the expensive run they configure;
and laws that mention context not yet in hand — data dimensions, live
resources — should be *declared* at construction and *checked* in one named
pass at the moment the context arrives, never guessed at and never skipped.

**Design failure representation and composition separately.** Conditions suit
contract violations and control flow that should stop. Computational result
values suit expected success or failure that callers compose as data. Domain
outcome families describe events such as denied authority, cancellation, or
completion. For each subsystem, separately specify whether failures
short-circuit or accumulate, which diagnostics survive, and where conditions
become values or values become conditions.

A computational result answers “did this calculation produce a value?” and
usually carries mechanics such as diagnostics or partial results. A domain
outcome answers “what happened in the modeled world?” and may represent
denial or cancellation even when the computation behaved perfectly. Keeping
those meanings apart prevents a business event from being mistaken for a bug,
or an implementation failure from becoming a permanent domain variant.

## Decision guides

The principles explain the defaults; the guides turn them into ordered
questions for a concrete design review.

Formulated as the questions to ask, in order, rather than flowcharts to
follow mechanically.

**Which object system?** Is it fundamentally a homogeneous vector that must
slice and live in data frames? — vctrs. Does it have identity and a lifetime,
with observers sharing its changes? — R6 or an environment. Is it a domain
value with laws and dispatchable behavior? — S7. Is it a veneer for ecosystem
politeness? — S3. Mixed answers mean a hybrid, which is normal.

**Which lifecycle policy?** Is ordinary revision through replacement part of
the concept? — editable value. Is it a completed fact whose public API should
forbid revision? — read-only snapshot. Must aliases observe the same evolving
resource or process? — reference owner. A value holding a reference is a
hybrid, not a deeply isolated value.

**Which sum-type encoding?** Do variants differ in fields, or does behavior
dispatch on them? — subclass family under an abstract parent. Do they differ
only in the tag? — enum-valued property. Is it several primitive shapes or
domain classes lawful in one slot? — union. Is the wire genuinely one bag
with conditional fields, variants are many and trivial, and dispatch is never
needed? — a discriminator plus class validator, chosen consciously as
denormalization.

**Which semantic-type tier?** Does the concept merely repeat a validation
shape across sites? — a reused property definition. Must it be impossible to
confuse with its base primitive, or does dispatch need it, while it remains
truly a primitive? — a class inheriting the base type. Does it have parts, or
operations of its own? — a composite class.

**Stored field, identity, or boundary-normalized?** Can two instances of the
class differ on it? If no — identity (computed property or
serializer-injected). If yes — must round-trips preserve the caller's exact
value? If yes — stored, with lenient parsing at the boundary and one
canonical stored form. Might the spec extend the value set? — stored enum
with a parse-time version gate.

**Where does a rule belong?** Does it mention one property's intrinsic shape
or value? — property contract. Several properties of one object? — class
validator. References among contained objects? — aggregate root. External
data, metadata, resources, or authority? — contextual operation.

**Condition, computational result, or domain outcome?** Is the event a
contract violation that should unwind control flow? — condition. Is expected
failure composed with a computation? — result value plus an explicit
short-circuit or accumulation protocol. Is the event meaningful in the
domain regardless of computation mechanics? — domain outcome family. Design
adapters among channels at named boundaries.

**Faithful conversion, adapter, compiler, or intermediate representation?**
Does the target preserve the same meaning pairwise? — `S7::convert()`. Is the
translation lossy, contextual, one-to-many, policy-bearing, or diagnostic? —
a named adapter or compiler. Have multiple real inputs or outputs exposed a
stable shared semantics? — consider an intermediate representation then, not
before.

**How deep should an embedded language go?** Does anything analyze or
transform the expressions, or target more than one output format? If no —
opaque passthrough, with the engine's validator as judge. Do humans
hand-write the expressions painfully? — constructor combinators (shallow
embedding). Is analysis, optimization, or multi-target translation the
product? — typed AST with generic passes (deep embedding). Representation as
deep as the analysis, and no deeper.

## Anti-pattern catalog

The guides identify a choice before implementation. The names below identify
the recurring failure shapes once code or a design proposal exists.

Named, so design reviews can point at them.

**Schema cosplay.** Mirroring incidental foreign structure as nominal domain
meaning without identifying the consumers or guarantees it serves. A
generated transport facade can be legitimate when flatness or exact fields
are authoritative; field count alone proves nothing. *Tell:* every foreign
interface becomes a hand-maintained class, yet downstream code still
interprets raw tags and nullable combinations.

**Validator soup.** The same law independently defined in the constructor,
property validator, class validator, and boundary schema. One authoritative
declaration may have several deliberate enforcements or projections; the
failure is duplicated authority with no agreement tests. *Tell:* fixing one
rule requires unrelated edits in several places.

**Shotgun parsing.** Input checks interleaved with processing across many
functions, no single point after which input is known-good, rejection
possible after side effects. *Tell:* `is.null()` and `is.character()` guards
deep in core logic; functions that "defensively" re-check their own
package's objects.

**Boolean blindness.** Check functions returning `TRUE`/`FALSE` whose
callers immediately need the *why* or the *what* — so they re-derive it.
*Tell:* `if (is_valid(x)) { ... }` followed by code that re-inspects `x` for
the very facts validity established. Return parsed evidence, not verdicts.

**The God validator.** One class validator enforcing property-local rules,
cross-property rules, and collection rules in a hundred lines. Placement
discipline lost; every rung's law in one place, none assumable by the others.
*Tell:* a class validator that re-checks types.

**Convert-everything.** Routing lossy, contextual, one-to-many translation
through a coercion generic because it exists. Coercion generics
(`S7::convert(from, to)`) suit faithful pairwise conversion; translation with
diagnostics, options, and asset generation deserves named functions with
room for a context argument and a report. *Tell:* a `convert` method with
side effects or a dozen options.

**Expression-system envy.** Re-implementing an engine's expression type
system in property validators — badly, partially, and forever chasing the
spec. The engine's validator owns rung 0. *Tell:* a validator that walks
nested lists interpreting operator names.

**Decorative hierarchy.** Inheritance introduced to share field names or to
"organize" classes that never dispatch differently. Dispatch will eventually
take the fake is-a seriously. *Tell:* an abstract parent with one child, or
parents whose children never appear in a method signature.

**The accidental reference owner.** Domain facts held in R6 "for
convenience," creating shared identity where observers did not need it.
*Tell:* `$clone()` calls sprinkled defensively and lifecycle tests for what
consumers treat as a value.

**Nullable confusion.** `NULL` doing triple duty as "required but not yet
supplied," "explicitly cleared," and "omitted on the wire," with no presence
policy. *Tell:* code that cannot distinguish an untouched field from a
cleared one; serializers with ad-hoc per-field `if (!is.null())` decisions.

**Premature DSL.** Combinators, quotation, and clever printing built before
any user wrote the target structures by hand long enough to reveal which
constructions are actually painful. The DSL then ossifies the wrong
abstractions. *Tell:* a DSL whose vocabulary mirrors the wire format
one-to-one instead of the domain's own idioms.

**Effectful getter.** A property that reads a file, calls an API, or mutates
a cache. Data access becomes action at a distance; cost and effects become
invisible at every `@`. *Tell:* property access inside a loop dominating a
profile; getters needing error handling.

**Boundary leakage.** Wire names, omit-empty decisions, or dialect quirks
appearing in core logic instead of the one serializer pair. *Tell:*
`"source-layer"` (the wire spelling) as a string anywhere except
`to_wire()`/`from_wire()`.

## A closing note on judgment

The principles compress experience, but they trade against each other in real
designs: parse-don't-validate argues for strictness at the boundary while
round-trip fidelity argues for permissive pass-through nodes; earned
abstraction argues for waiting while semantic atoms argue for naming meanings
early; shallow hierarchies argue against intermediate classes while shared
schema sometimes argues for them. The earlier documents exist so that when
two principles collide, the *reasons* behind each are available and the
trade can be made explicitly, on the record, instead of by whichever slogan
was remembered first.
